These results help researchers and practitioners select suitable metrics, interpret metric values, and compare blockchain systems with respect to trade-offs among DoD, scalability, and security.
item.dc:creator: Mansur Masama Aliyu, Niclas Kannengie{\ss}er, Ali Sunyaev

item.title: Watermark Robustness and Radioactivity May Be at Odds in Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2510.17033v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) across distributed data sources. As these sources increasingly include LLM-generated text, provenance tracking becomes essential for accountability and transparency. We adapt LLM watermarking for FL data provenance, where a subset of clients computes local updates on watermarked data, and the server averages all updates into the global LLM. We find that several evaluated LLM watermarks remain radioactive in this setup: the watermark signal stays detectable after fine-tuning, with a $p-$value reaching $10^{-24}$ even when only 6.6% of data is watermarked. However, the server can act as an active adversary, aiming to preserve model utility while evading provenance tracking. We observe that updates from watermarked synthetic data appear as outliers relative to clean updates. Our adversary thus applies strong robust aggregation to filter out these outliers along with the watermark signal. All evaluated radioactive watermarks are not robust against such an adversarial server. Our work suggests fundamental trade-offs between radioactivity, robustness, and utility.
item.dc:creator: Leixu Huang, Zedian Shao, Teodora Baluta

item.title: Expected Harm: Rethinking Safety Evaluation of (Mis)Aligned LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2602.01600v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current evaluations of LLM safety predominantly rely on severity-based taxonomies to assess the harmfulness of models' responses to malicious queries. We argue that this formulation requires re-examination as it implicitly equates model output with realized harm while neglecting Execution Likelihood-the conditional probability of a threat being realized by a real-world actor given a model's response. In this work, we introduce Expected Harm, a metric that weights the severity of a jailbreak by its execution likelihood, modeled as a function of execution cost. Through empirical analysis of state-of-the-art models, we reveal a systematic Inverse Risk Calibration: models disproportionately exhibit stronger refusal behaviors for low-likelihood (high-cost) threats while remaining vulnerable to high-likelihood (low-cost) queries. Mechanistically, we first provide an analysis using linear probing, revealing that while refusal mechanisms linearly separate queries by severity, they do not use execution likelihood as an indicator for refusal. Then, we use Olmo-3's open-source staged checkpoints to trace the root cause of miscalibration to the Supervised Fine Tuning (SFT) training data distribution (82.8% of safety examples at cost levels 0-1) and show that cost representations are weak from the SFT stage onward. Finally, we demonstrate that this miscalibration creates a vulnerability: by exploiting this property, we increase the attack success rate of existing jailbreaks by up to $2\times$.
item.dc:creator: Yen-Shan Chen, Zhi Rui Tam, Cheng-Kuang Wu, Yun-Nung Chen

item.title: STRIATUM-CTF: A Protocol-Driven Agentic Framework for Autonomous CTF Solving
item.description: arXiv:2603.22577v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous cyber operations increasingly depend on agents that can chain reconnaissance, exploitation, and analysis across many tools while maintaining state over long task horizons. Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising orchestrators for this workflow, but naive agents that pipe model output directly into a shell are brittle: they emit malformed commands, hallucinate non-existent command-line options or packages, and lose track of earlier findings as the context window fills. We present STRIATUM-CTF, a modular agentic framework for Capture-the-Flag (CTF) solving that mediates between LLM reasoning and tool execution using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Offensive-security tools are exposed as strictly typed, schema-validated functions; the protocol layer rejects out-of-schema tool calls before execution and returns structured observations that the agent uses to self-correct. We evaluate the system in two ways. In a controlled study of 180 runs across 15 CTF challenges under four levels of attached procedural documentation, the system succeeds on 77.8-86.7% of attempts; notably, a schema-only configuration with no procedural documentation already reaches 77.8%, and no condition differs significantly from another. In a single live, multi-team CTF at Florida State University, the system placed first against a field of more than 30 registered teams -- a single, non-replicated event decided by a 10-point margin over the runner-up, and therefore a demonstration of feasibility rather than of superiority over human experts. Because all four ablation conditions share the same tool layer, our controlled study isolates documentation volume rather than the protocol layer itself; we accordingly present schema-mediated grounding as a design principle with qualitative support rather than as a measured effect.
item.dc:creator: James Hugglestone, Samuel Jacob Chacko, Dawson Stoller, Ryan Schmidt, Xiuwen Liu

item.title: A Survey on Long-Term Memory Security in LLM Agents: Attacks, Defenses, and Governance Across the Memory Lifecycle
item.description: arXiv:2604.16548v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The emergence of writable, cross-session persistent memory in LLM agents introduces a qualitatively different threat landscape from conventional input-centric security concerns, characterized by three properties: persistence, statefulness, and propagation. To systematically characterize this landscape, we propose a Memory Lifecycle Framework that organizes attacks, defenses, and their cross-phase dependencies along two axes: six lifecycle phases (Write, Store, Retrieve, Execute, Share & Propagate, Forget & Rollback) and four security objectives (Integrity, Confidentiality, Availability, Governance). This analysis in turn exposes the need for explicit security requirements at the system level, motivating Verifiable Memory Governance (VMG), a framework of five architectural primitives for specifying and evaluating auditable, recoverable control over memory state within declared system and threat-model boundaries. Our analysis motivates integrating provenance, versioning, and policy-aware retention with retrieval and execution defenses to support auditable prevention, containment, and recovery across the lifecycle.
item.dc:creator: Zehao Lin, Xixuan Hao, Renyu Fu, Shaobo Cui, Kai Chen, Chunyu Li, Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong

item.title: Multimodal User Authentication via Keystroke-Triggered Fusion of Glove-Based Finger Pressure and Hand Kinematics
item.description: arXiv:2607.24747v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Keystroke dynamics constitute a cost-effective behavioral biometric, but their timing features degrade under environmental and hardware variation. We replace these features with 19 dimensions of finger pressure and hand kinematics, sampled around each keystroke by a custom data glove - ten piezoresistive pressure sensors and a nine-axis inertial measurement unit (IMU). The two modalities are encoded by separate convolutional neural network-long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) branches and joined only at the embedding. We collected typing data from ten participants, one enrolled as the genuine user. Training uses a desktop keyboard and evaluation a laptop keyboard recorded on a later day; the held-out impostor is excluded from training, and each of the nine takes that role in turn (Leave-One-Impostor-Out). Under this condition the method attains a mean Equal Error Rate (EER) of $0.53 \pm 0.42$% after three consecutive keystrokes, about 0.77 s of typing at the measured median pace, and $0.18 \pm 0.22$% after five. Results depend strongly on which impostor is held out. A per-modality ablation finds the fused model significantly better than both single-modality models at every smoothing window. The pressure-level channels carry that advantage and have to be scale-matched to deliver it, by separate encoders or by standardization indifferently.
item.dc:creator: Issei Hyakuda, Lei Jing

item.title: The Guard That Cried Wolf: How Scary Words Make Agent Guardrails Refuse Legitimate Actions
item.description: arXiv:2608.27009v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent guardrails are checks that approve or refuse each action before an LLM executes it. Sometimes they refuse requests that are genuinely safe. This over-safety blocks deployment when a guardrail refuses an authorized task. Evaluating over-safety is hard: at the boundary an authorized action resembles an unauthorized one, and the safe-versus-unsafe label is a choice of authorization policy, not fixed by the action alone. We argue it therefore requires a benchmark that does not yet exist, one that maps the decision boundary of an ideal guardrail. Harvesting such a benchmark from real data is impractical: boundary cases are hard to collect, their labels hard to verify. The gap is real, so we construct Cautious Bench, the first benchmark to make over-safety the construct for agent guardrails; it codesigns each sample and its label with a stated authorization policy. A build-time gate re-derives every example to certify it, so each label is a mechanical consequence of the policy rather than an annotator's per-sample verdict, a reference against which researchers can measure real guardrails. The benchmark renders 756 Decidable benign/twin pairs, each under three object-name types (2,268 measured pairs), and 40 Undecidable pairs reported separately. Measuring six guardrails from five designs, we find a name-superstition effect: each over-refuses an authorized action more often under a scary-looking object name than a benign one. Since only the object name varies in the aforementioned contrast experiments, the deviation is the name's doing: the guardrails read the surface label, not the authorization context.
item.dc:creator: Yingjie Zhang, Yuanbo Xie, Kai Chen

item.title: A Unified Attack Framework against Statistical Generative Watermarks for Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.27653v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Watermarking has emerged as a key tool for identifying text generated by large language models (LLMs), with current schemes embedding statistical signals into the generation process to enable later detection. In this work, we identify a shared weakness across a broad class of popular LLM watermarking methods, including KGW (and its variants), GumbelSoft, DipMark, ITS, and SynthID. We show that these schemes exhibit a fundamental link between their detection scores and the token probability shifts they introduce during generation. This link, which we call score-ratio alignment, allows an attacker with only black-box query access to the model--and no knowledge of secret keys or model weights--to produce text that evades detection while remaining fluent and natural. We prove that the resulting attack is optimal across all covered watermark families, and show that the weakness is intrinsic: any watermark designed to maximize statistical detection power necessarily induces the very structure that attackers can exploit. We evaluate our attack on seven popular generative LLM watermarking schemes, three LLMs, and tasks, which reduce detection rates to at most 0.05 across all settings while preserving text quality. Our findings show that current watermarking methods can be reliably defeated under realistic attack conditions, highlighting the need for fundamentally different watermarking designs that decouple detection scores from token probability shifts.
item.dc:creator: Romina Omidi, Nima Naderloui, Yuan Hong, Binghui Wang

item.title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
item.description: arXiv:2610.35835v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly. We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent. To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities. We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels

item.title: Janus Vehicles: Entity-Centric Threat Modelling of Protocol-Conformant Vehicles under a Malicious-Manufacturer Assumption
item.description: arXiv:2610.37059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automotive cybersecurity commonly assumes benign end-product manufacturers and design authorities, focusing on supply-chain threats, external attacks, and compromised network participants observable through misbehaviour. This assumption overlooks malicious-by-design vehicles that remain authentic and protocol-conformant while performing undeclared sensing, communication, or context-triggered actuation. We formulate an Entity-Centric Threat Model spanning three subcomponents. The first, Malign Entity Archetypes, describes four types of malign entity: peer-benign, purpose-malicious vehicles; compromised vehicles; reappropriated genuine components; and imitated vehicles or components. The model exposes two assurance gaps: authenticity does not establish declared-purpose conformance, while malicious functionality can evade detection based on behavioural history or peer-visible evidence. Reappropriated components can remain genuine and retain usable identities or capabilities outside authorised contexts, reducing the effectiveness of signal fingerprinting and certificate-based authentication. To structure this threat space, we introduce a Behaviour-Locus Matrix that maps covert, overt, and concealment actions across hardware, software, and network loci. For peer-benign, purpose-malicious vehicles, we further present a Behavioural Interaction Model that represents how hidden capabilities are contextually activated, realised through actions, manifested within the vehicle and its environment, and potentially observed or concealed.
item.dc:creator: Jaeung Franciskus Yoo, Huy Kang Kim

item.title: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense
item.description: arXiv:2610.37415v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prior work framed the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent, but did not examine the effects of label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffolds, or existing memories. Following its GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D adjudication, this paper takes the A2A-TIBA attack as the test vehicle and the semantic breach rate as the primary indicator, and characterizes the security boundary of the envelope layer through a 2x2 factorial experiment, a memory experiment, and control experiments (an unlabeled same-protocol baseline, a one-day interleaved control, and benign tasks). The results show that, under authentic envelopes, strong labels consistently reduce the semantic breach rate (-56 to -61 percentage points), and the benefit of weak labels is about a quarter to a half of that of strong labels; forging the envelope weakens the strong label's benefit (interaction OR = 2.10, p = 0.022) and its direction varies across frontends; the effect of memory valence exceeds that of any label manipulation; success memory raises the semantic breach rate and failure memory lowers it, while most conflict combinations return to the no-memory baseline; the interleaved control reproduces the direction that "unlabeled is worst"; and on benign tasks the cost of strong labels appears in layers across frontends and backends. Accordingly, this paper extends the envelope layer into "admission surface plus context assembly surface," whose security boundary is a dynamic outcome jointly shaped by label claims, frontend permissions, and historical memory.
item.dc:creator: Yuelin Han

item.title: SoK: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Taxonomy, Architectures, Evaluation, and Research Directions
item.description: arXiv:2603.07379v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly evolving into agentic architectures where large language models autonomously coordinate multi-step reasoning, dynamic memory management, and iterative retrieval strategies. Despite rapid industrial adoption, current research lacks a systematic understanding of Agentic RAG as a sequential decision-making system, leading to highly fragmented architectures, inconsistent evaluation methodologies, and unresolved reliability risks. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) paper provides the first unified framework for understanding these autonomous systems. We formalize agentic retrieval-generation loops as finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes, explicitly modeling their control policies and state transitions. Building upon this formalization, we develop a comprehensive taxonomy and modular architectural decomposition that categorizes systems by their planning mechanisms, retrieval orchestration, memory paradigms, and tool-invocation behaviors. We further analyze the critical limitations of traditional static evaluation practices and identify severe systemic risks inherent to autonomous loops, including compounding hallucination propagation, memory poisoning, retrieval misalignment, and cascading tool-execution vulnerabilities. Finally, we outline key doctoral-scale research directions spanning stable adaptive retrieval, cost-aware orchestration, formal trajectory evaluation, and oversight mechanisms, providing a definitive roadmap for building reliable, controllable, and scalable agentic retrieval systems.
item.dc:creator: Saroj Mishra, Suman Niroula, Umesh Yadav, Dilip Thakur, Srijan Gyawali, Shiva Gaire

item.title: Inadvertent Context Leakage in Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.19857v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For AI agents to be useful beyond simple chat, they must hold sensitive user context such as calendars, credentials, health records, and financial data. We study whether the mere presence of such secrets in a model's context window introduces hidden correlations into the model's benign outputs, allowing reconstruction even when the model correctly refuses direct extraction. We further study whether an adversary can actively engineer prompts that amplify this effect, using the model as a covert carrier to transmit secrets through seemingly innocuous text. In both cases, this limited leakage is exploited using a novel adaptive attack that assumes black-box access to the underlying model. In controlled experiments across eight proprietary models, we find that 2-digit in-context secrets are reconstructed with near-perfect accuracy and 4-digit secrets at 82\% exact match, all from outputs the model produces in response to ordinary, non-adversarial requests. We observe that more capable models leak more: stronger instruction-following amplifies sensitivity to in-context secrets, suggesting leakage is a byproduct of capability as opposed to a patchable bug. We show this leakage enables two practical attacks: (1) a trained classifier that infers semantic predicates about user memories (e.g., health conditions, financial events) from routine natural-language outputs, and (2) an RL-trained adversary that extracts full Social Security Numbers from a production-style agent.
item.dc:creator: Jaiden Fairoze, Neal Mangaokar, Kamalika Chaudhuri, Sanjam Garg, Saeed Mahloujifar

item.title: Do User-Authored Permission Policies Improve Protection Against AI Agent Overreach?
item.description: arXiv:2608.27443v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI agents are poised to become a primary interface to digital products, acting across email, files, payments, and personal data. People without professional software backgrounds need understandable, reusable ways to control actions across services. We examine a mechanism in which a language model maps actions to plain-language consequence categories with user-authored "allow", "ask", or "never" rules. We ask what is gained and lost when decisions are made in advance as reusable rules rather than separately for each action. We analyzed 113 participants without professional software backgrounds across three conditions: per-action human-in-the-loop approval (HITL), automated per-action model review (AUTO), or user-authored consequence policy (POLICY). Participants judged 2 examples in each of 4 consequence categories; POLICY participants then set one rule per category. All supervised an 18-action simulated day, including 7 overreach actions. POLICY blocked less overreach than HITL (-20.1 percentage points, 95% CI [-32.1, -8.1]) and AUTO (-14.5 points, 95% CI [-25.8, -3.2]). POLICY lowered runtime prompts from 18.0 to 10.9, but total intervention time was not reliably lower when rule setup was included. Exploratory analysis showed that participants chose "ask" for 114 of 140 POLICY rules, returning most overreach actions to runtime. Of the 148 overreach actions executed in POLICY, 133 followed human approval and 15 ran automatically under "allow" rules. Across all 7 overreach actions, POLICY had the highest approval rate. Counterintuitively, user-authored rules did not by themselves provide stronger protection: many actions outside users' original requests went through after users approved them. These results reveal a gap between preference and commitment: repeatedly choosing "ask" preserves case-by-case choice but prevents a standing policy from settling decisions in advance.
item.dc:creator: Ting Yan

item.title: Can Agentic Code Review Catch Vulnerabilities Before They Are Merged?
item.description: arXiv:2610.33509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. In this paper, we present SecPRBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic security review on validated real-world code changes. More specifically, we have built an automated agentic pipeline to autonomously harvest, build, and validate massive real-world bug-introducing commits for popular software systems. To ensure precise evaluation, we also adopt LLM-as-a-judge to credit the findings matching ground-truth vulnerabilities. To date, we have collected 265 tasks from nine critical systems, including Firefox, V8, and OpenSSL with millions of lines of code. Across eight frontier models, recall ranges from 32.5% to 78.1%, with Grok 4.6 and GPT-6 sol ranking at the top. Our study also shows that most misses are not simply oversights: in 68% of them, the agent reports on a file that holds the flaw but argues for a different mechanism. Security-focused harnesses also behave differently: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers recall by 8.3 points, mostly by abstaining, while Anthropic's Defending Code harness raises it by 7.7 points, at a higher cost.
item.dc:creator: Yihan Yang, Chenyuan Yang, Zijie Zhao, Anh Nguyen Hoang, Ziqi Zhang, Weidong Wang, Zhiheng Lyu, Lingming Zhang

item.title: A Rowhammer attack on Fil-C's software capabilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.33748v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fil-C retrofits spatial and temporal memory safety onto C/C++ using software capabilities (bounds that are checked at every pointer dereference). Fil-C's guarantee rests on an unstated hardware assumption: that DRAM preserves the capabilities. We show that Rowhammer breaks it. In Fil-C 0.679 a part of each heap pointer's capability lives in a 16-byte header stored inline in ordinary DRAM immediately before the object pointed to, with no mechanism to prevent capabilities from corruption. A single 0 → 1 bit flip in the capability's upper-bound expands the pointer's permitted range by 2k bytes and is invisible to the runtime, raising no panic or signal. We demonstrate this by using Fil-C to convert existing Rowhammer attacks into concrete attacks against a heterogeneous collection of victim software. To aid reproducibility (not everybody has DRAM vulnerable to Rowhammer) we split our demonstration into two paths. First, along a deterministic path, we isolate Fil-C as a novel attack vector using a deterministic, Rowhammer-like fault-injection model. Across four case studies, this model corrupts the upper-bound word of a pointer, permitting previously out-of-bounds reads and writes. We use this to achieve a bounded read/write window, secret disclosure, privilege escalation by flipping an adjacent is_admin field, and the leakage of a tenant API key in a multi-tenant credential service backed by SQLite (compiled under Fil-C). Second, along a physical end-to-end path, we demonstrate all four attacks on real hardware equipped with DDR3 memory, and with Target Row Refresh (TRR) equipped DDR4, proving the exploits are physically realisable. The latter attack shows that the TRR defence does not close the Fil-C delivery channel. We close with a discussion of Fil-C-specific mitigations.
item.dc:creator: Amir Naseredini, Suhas Viswanath, Martin Berger

item.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.37239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-relational graph detectors learn from clean data how much to trust each relation, but an adversary pays a different price to manipulate each relation and each action; taking such costs as given, we ask when using a relation is worse than ignoring it. Our first main result proves that degree gating strictly beats every selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, and that this window is sharp; on real graphs, validated gating gains exactly on the relations that meet these conditions and nowhere else. Our second shows that a per-node exposure bound, which extends to message passing, tells a platform which relation to harden: exposure per unit cost, computed without any attack, picks the relation whose hardening raises the exact trap threshold most in 15 of 16 cases, against at most 7 for informativeness, cheapness, or an analysis with equal edit costs. Supporting tools give exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for R-GCN and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation, under which clean-trained graph detectors fall below their graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs. A selection protocol built on these results is never significantly worse than ignoring the graph; with at most four relations it mostly abstains, as validation alone would, and its cost-aware proposals help when relations are many, so far shown on synthetic graphs. Without cost information, the safe choice is to abstain.
item.dc:creator: Vincess Dongmo, Astride Melvin Fokam Ninyim

item.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
item.description: arXiv:2610.37657v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.
